name: Kikuyu
confidence_why: Four first-hand descriptions (Hinde 1904, McGregor 1905, Barlow 1914 and Armstrong 1940, the standard phonetic study of the language) all put a weak stress on the penultimate syllable, and the one dissent, Philippson 1991, is a comparative survey that files Kikuyu as purely tonal, a statement about the type of prosodic system that does not place the stress anywhere else.

catalog_quote: STRESS. Main Stress. The general rule is that the last syllable but one (penultimate syllable) bears the main accent, though frequently the stress is so light as to be scarcely distinguishable. Exs. nyũ'mba; kĩhā'to; nĩngamwo'na; gũthiũrũrũ'ka. Effect of Suffix. The stress may be shifted because of the addition of a suffix or suffixes. Ex. ako'me, akoma'ge, akomagĩ're. Effect of Monosyllables. In certain cases a word of one syllable following another word is closely joined to it in pronunciation and causes the accent to fall on the last syllable of that word. ... Syllable consisting of Vowel only. In Kikuyu, a syllable consisting of a vowel only, always tends to be absorbed by the preceding syllable; so that when the last syllable of a word consists of a vowel only, the stress is generally on the third last syllable (antepenultimate), not on the second last. In such words as kũ-rĩ-a, a-…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Kikuyu is not in the catalog. Of the five title hits, only Philippson 1991 (Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East Bantu) is about this language's prosody; it is print-only (theses.fr 'accessible: non'), and its abstract classes Kikuyu as 'pleinement tonale' at the opposite pole from penultimate-demarcative-accent languages like Swahili — a mild tension with the older grammars. Wagacha et al. 2006 (downloaded, read) is orthographic diacritic restoration with no prosody content; Dybo 1994, Feldstein 1978 and Kiparsky 2010 are Saharan/Slavic/Indo-European accentology attached to Kikuyu by Glottolog's computerized keyword 'paradigmatic' (Dybo's record says so explicitly). Best first-hand statement read: Barlow 1914 p.6 (page image verified) — weak penultimate main stress, final vowel-only syllable absorbed so surface antepenult, shifts under suffixes/enclitics/emphasis; corroborated by McGregor 1905, Hinde 1904 and the Armstrong 1940 §516 snippet already held by the project. Acquisition list of works to obtain: Armstrong 1940 ch. XXIII (snippet only) and Philippson 1991 (medium).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened the page image (Google Books full view id 9TK4O0lNrD0C, printed p.6 'INTRODUCTION') and read it directly, not just the scanned. The quoted passage is there verbatim under the heading 'STRESS. / Main Stress.': 'The general rule is that the last syllable but one (penultimate syllable) bears the main accent, though frequently the stress is so light as to be scarcely distinguishable. Exs. nyũ'mba; kĩhā'to; nĩngamwo'na; gũthiũrũrũ'ka.' followed by 'Effect of Suffix. The stress may be shifted because of the addition of a suffix or suffixes. Ex. ako'me, akoma'ge, akomagĩ're.' the first reader's '[..]' elides the 'Effect of Monosyllables' paragraph (Ikara' thĩ; akĩĩgi'ta na' ngo), and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Weak main stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (recomputed over the whole word as suffixes are added); where the word ends in a bare-vowel syllable (…C V-V), that vowel is absorbed into the preceding syllable so stress surfaces on the antepenult; stress is independent of the (contrastive) tone system and is often barely perceptible. Corroborated by McGregor 1905 p.13 ('In the majority of cases the accent falls on the penultimate syllable') and by Armstrong 1940 section 516 (snippet: 'A weak stress occurs generally on the penultimate syllable, and is independent of tone… often so weak that… it is impossible to distinguish it').
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described (Barlow speaks only of 'main stress'/'main accent').
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions to the vowel-absorption (antepenult) sub-rule: ĩtĩ'a 'be conceited', iri'a 'milk', tense forms of thi'ĩ 'go', gĩ'a 'have', tu'a 'break', &c; a closely joined following monosyllable draws the accent onto the final syllable of the preceding word (Ikara' thĩ; akĩĩgi'ta na' ngo); stress 'freely changed in conversation for the sake of emphasis and rhetorical effect', often with vowel lengthening; 'Sometimes the main stress may be changed from the penultimate position in interrogation' (p.6-7); enclitics rĩ and ĩ 'do not usually affect the position of the stress' (p.8); 'The above rules being only general and exceptions numerous all important deviations are marked in the vocabularies' (p.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on citation forms, but with phrase-level perturbations (following monosyllables, emphasis, interrogation). Kikuyu is a two-tone + downstep language (Armstrong 1940; Clements 1984; Englebretson & Wa-Ngatho 2015); all three sources that mention stress (McGregor 1905, Barlow 1914, Armstrong 1940 snippet) call it weak/light and penultimate, and modern descriptions discuss tone only.
new_statements.identity_note: Barlow 1914 describes Kikuyu as used at the Church of Scotland mission (standard orthography of the United Kikuyu Language Committee); no dialect is singled out, so it maps to kiku1240 at language level. McGregor 1905 (CMS) likewise language-level. Githinji 2014 (silent on stress) is specifically the Ki-Ndia dialect (Kirinyaga). Armstrong 1940 is based on one educated speaker (per Clements 1984).

Exs. nyũ'mba; kĩhã'to; nĩngamwo'na; gũthiũrũrũ'ka. [...] In Kikuyu, a syllable consisting of a vowel only, always tends to be absorbed by the preceding syllable; so that when the last syllable of a word consists of a vowel only, the stress is generally on the third last syllable (antepenultimate), not on the second last.
new_statements.citation: Barlow, A. Ruffell (1914). Tentative Studies in Kikuyu Grammar and Idiom. Edinburgh: William Blackwood & Sons (Foreign Mission Committee of the Church of Scotland). Introduction, STRESS, p.6.
new_statements.locator: p.6, 'STRESS. Main Stress' and 'Syllable consisting of Vowel only'
new_statements.reading: Weak, largely non-contrastive penultimate stress (phonologically fixed-penultimate), counted over surface syllables with a final vowel-only syllable merging into the preceding one (so antepenultimate on the orthographic count); shifts under suffixation, enclisis of following monosyllables, and rhetorical emphasis. Independently corroborated by McGregor 1905 p.13 ('In the majority of cases the accent falls on the penultimate syllable'), Hinde 1904 p.ix ('The accent almost invariably falls on the penultimate'), and — snippet only — Armstrong 1940 §516 ('A weak stress occurs generally on the penultimate syllable, and is independent of tone'). Philippson 1991 (abstract) instead files Kikuyu as fully tonal without a demarcative penultimate accent; that thesis is the one unread source that could refine the picture.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

new_statements.quote: We find a one end purely tonal systems (like kikuyu) and at the other end systems with purely demarcative penultimate stress, with all intermediate cases. [FR: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés.]
new_statements.translation: These systems in fact range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with a demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), all intermediate cases being represented.

The abstract also states the diachronic hypothesis that the emergence of a demarcative penultimate accent (serving as the domain limit…
new_statements.relation_note: Differs in TYPE, not placement: the catalog files Kikuyu as fixed-penultimate stress, while Philippson's typology puts Kikuyu at the 'purely tonal' extreme, explicitly opposed to demarcative penultimate accent. The two are reconcilable through Armstrong 1940 §516 (weak, non-contrastive penultimate stress independent of tone), but the abstract alone denies Kikuyu an accentual (penultimate) system. Abstract only; the 542-page thesis body was not obtained (SUDOC print record only).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kikuyu is placed at the 'purely tonal' pole of the East African Bantu prosodic continuum, opposite languages with purely demarcative penultimate stress (Swahili); i.e. the thesis classes Kikuyu as a tone language without a demarcative penultimate accent. No placement rule for stress is given in the abstract.
new_statements.identity_note: No listed work describes a particular Kikuyu dialect; Cysouw 2001 does not treat Kikuyu at all (its Narrow Bantu example is Nkosi, Cameroon). Philippson 1991 refers to 'kikuyu' generically.

readall_conflicts: Only one of the three works yields anything, and only as an abstract: Philippson 1991 classes Kikuyu as a 'purely tonal' system at the opposite pole from demarcative penultimate stress, which is a typological disagreement with the catalog's fixed-penultimate record. It is not a placement conflict: the first-hand sources already held by the project (Barlow 1914 p.6, McGregor 1905 p.13, Hinde 1904 p.ix, and Armstrong 1940 §516 in snippet) all put a weak, non-contrastive stress on the penultimate syllable and Armstrong states it is independent of tone, so Philippson's classification is about the prosodic system type (tone, not accent), which is compatible with a phonetically weak penultimate stress. Mugane 1997 could not be opened (lending-only) and Cysouw 2001 is not about Kikuyu.

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale. [EN: These systems range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with penultimate demarcative accent (Swahili), with all intermediate cases represented ... the main driver of evolution was the emergence of a penultimate demarcative accent serving as domain edge for tone association.]
sources.note: Abstract only: places Kikuyu at the 'fully tonal' pole of East Bantu, opposite languages with penultimate demarcative stress (Swahili). Implies Kikuyu lacks a demarcative penultimate accent in his typology — a mild tension with Barlow 1914 / McGregor 1905 / Armstrong 1940, which all report a (weak) penultimate stress. The thesis body (30 languages, Kikuyu among the tagged lgcodes) is not online: theses.fr 'accessible: non', HAL no record, Glottolog lists the file only as an internal copy.
